questions.stem: A frame of reference is described as inertial when it:
options: is fixed to the centre of the Earth, so it is the only true rest frame
is at rest or moving at constant velocity, so Newton's first law holds in it
is accelerating uniformly, so objects in it have a constant acceleration
is rotating at a steady rate, so its speed never changes
questions.explanation: In an inertial frame, an object with no net force on it stays at rest or moves at constant velocity. A rotating frame is accelerating, because its direction of motion keeps changing, even if its speed is steady. Special relativity holds that there is no single true rest frame.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-inertial frame of reference?
options: A spacecraft drifting at constant velocity in deep space
A lift moving upward at a constant speed
A car braking hard at a red light
A train moving at a steady 80 km h⁻¹ on a straight track
questions.explanation: A braking car is decelerating, so objects inside seem to lurch forward with no force pushing them, and Newton's first law appears to fail. The other frames move at constant velocity, so they are inertial.

questions.stem: A passenger in a train with no windows hangs a pendulum from the ceiling. It hangs straight down. What can the passenger conclude?
options: The train must be moving forward, because the pendulum is not swinging
The train is accelerating, because only acceleration keeps the pendulum still
The train is moving at constant velocity or at rest, but they cannot tell which
The train must be at rest, because the pendulum would tilt if the train were moving
questions.explanation: In any inertial frame the laws of physics are the same, so no experiment inside the closed train can distinguish rest from constant velocity. The pendulum would hang at an angle only if the train were accelerating, which would make it a non-inertial frame.

questions.stem: According to Einstein's first postulate of special relativity:
options: nothing with mass can travel faster than the speed of sound
time passes at the same rate in all frames of reference
the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference
the speed of light depends on the motion of its source
questions.explanation: The first postulate, the principle of relativity, says no inertial frame is special: every law of physics, including electromagnetism, takes the same form in all of them. Time passing at the same rate in all frames is the classical assumption that relativity overturned.

questions.stem: Einstein's second postulate of special relativity states that:
options: light in a vacuum has the same speed for all observers, whatever the source's motion
the speed of light in a vacuum depends on how fast the observer is moving towards the source
light needs a medium, the aether, to travel through, which is at rest in space
the speed of light is the same in all materials, including glass and water
questions.explanation: Every inertial observer measures light in a vacuum travelling at c, about 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, regardless of how the source or observer moves. Light travels more slowly in glass and water, and special relativity does not need an aether.

questions.stem: A spacecraft travelling at 0.50c towards Earth switches on its headlights. At what speed does an observer on Earth measure the light approaching?
options: 2c
c
questions.explanation: By the second postulate, the speed of light in a vacuum is c for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of the source. Adding velocities in the everyday way gives 1.5c, but that classical rule fails at speeds near c.

questions.stem: A lamp in the exact centre of a train carriage flashes. In the train's frame, the light reaches the front and back walls at the same time. For an observer on the platform, as the train moves forward at high speed:
options: the light reaches both walls at once, because simultaneity is the same in all frames
the light never reaches the front wall, because the wall moves away at nearly c
the light reaches the back wall first, because the back wall moves towards the light
the light reaches the front wall first, because the light is carried forward by the train
questions.explanation: The platform observer also sees light travel at c in both directions, but the back wall moves towards its flash and the front wall moves away, so the light reaches the back first. Events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another. The light is not carried forward by the train, because its speed is c in every frame.

questions.stem: What does the train-carriage thought experiment show about simultaneity?
options: Whether two separated events happen at the same time depends on the observer's frame
Two events are simultaneous only if they happen at the same place in every frame
Simultaneity is absolute, but moving clocks run at different rates in each frame
Simultaneity depends only on how far each observer is from the two events
questions.explanation: Because light travels at c in every frame, observers in relative motion disagree about whether separated events occur at the same moment. This is a real disagreement about when events happen, not an effect of the light's travel time, which each observer has already allowed for.

questions.stem: In a light clock, a pulse bounces between two mirrors. The clock moves sideways at high speed past an observer. Why does the observer measure each tick taking longer?
options: The pulse follows a longer diagonal path in the observer's frame but still travels at c
The pulse travels more slowly in the observer's frame, so it takes longer between mirrors
The mirrors move further apart when the clock moves, making the path longer
The pulse is dragged backward by the moving clock, so it takes longer to arrive
questions.explanation: In the clock's own frame the pulse goes straight up and down. In the observer's frame the mirrors move sideways, so the pulse travels a longer zigzag path. Light has the same speed c in both frames, so the longer path takes more time and the moving clock runs slow. The mirror separation is perpendicular to the motion, so it is not contracted.

questions.stem: What is proper time?
options: The time measured by an atomic clock that is kept on the Earth's surface
The time between two events measured by a clock present at both events
The time between two events measured by an observer moving at the speed of light
The longest possible time between two events, measured in any frame
questions.explanation: Proper time, t₀, is measured in the frame where the two events happen at the same place, such as by a clock carried with a moving particle. Every other inertial observer measures a longer time, t, so proper time is the shortest interval, not the longest.

questions.stem: A spacecraft passes Earth at 0.80c. An astronaut on board measures 6.0 s between two ticks of her clock. How long between those ticks does an observer on Earth measure?
questions.explanation: t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²) = 6.0/√(1 − 0.64) = 6.0/0.60 = 10 s. The ticks happen at the same place on the ship, so 6.0 s is the proper time and Earth measures a longer, dilated time. Multiplying by 0.60 instead of dividing gives 3.6 s.

questions.stem: Muons made in the upper atmosphere have a mean lifetime of 2.2 µs in their own frame. They travel at 0.995c, for which the Lorentz factor is 10. What mean lifetime does an observer on the ground measure?
options: 2.2 µs
4.4 µs
22 µs
questions.explanation: The muon's own lifetime, 2.2 µs, is the proper time. A ground observer measures t = γt₀ = 10 × 2.2 µs = 22 µs. Dividing by the Lorentz factor instead gives 0.22 µs, which mixes up which observer measures the proper time.

questions.stem: Muons with a proper mean lifetime of 2.2 µs travel at 0.995c. Without relativity they would travel about 660 m on average before decaying. Why do many reach the ground from over 10 km up?
options: In Earth's frame they gain mass as they fall, so gravity pulls them down more quickly
In Earth's frame their lifetime is dilated to about 22 µs, so they go about 6.6 km
In Earth's frame they travel faster than light, so they cover 10 km in under 2.2 µs
In Earth's frame their lifetime is shortened to about 0.22 µs, so they slow down less
questions.explanation: With γ ≈ 10, Earth observers measure the lifetime as about 22 µs, so the average distance is about 0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 22 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 6.6 km, and many muons survive the trip. In the muon's frame the same result appears as length contraction of the atmosphere. Nothing travels faster than light.

questions.stem: At what speed is the Lorentz factor, γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), equal to 2?
questions.explanation: γ = 2 means √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.5, so 1 − v²/c² = 0.25 and v²/c² = 0.75, giving v = √0.75 c ≈ 0.87c. Stopping at v²/c² = 0.75 gives 0.75c, and assuming γ = 2 at half the speed of light gives 0.50c.

questions.stem: Why are relativistic effects not noticed in everyday life?
options: Relativity applies only to light, not to objects made of matter
Relativistic effects cancel out when objects move in circles
Earth's gravity prevents time dilation from happening on its surface
At everyday speeds v²/c² is tiny, so the Lorentz factor is almost exactly 1
questions.explanation: Even at 0.1c, γ is only about 1.005, and everyday speeds are millions of times smaller than c, so the differences from classical physics are far too small to notice without very precise clocks. Relativity applies to all matter, as muons and moving atomic clocks show.

questions.stem: A star is 4.0 light-years from Earth. A spacecraft travels there at 0.80c. How long does the trip take according to Earth clocks and according to the crew's clocks?
options: 5.0 years on Earth and 3.0 years for the crew
3.0 years on Earth and 5.0 years for the crew
5.0 years on Earth and 5.0 years for the crew
4.0 years on Earth and 2.4 years for the crew
questions.explanation: In Earth's frame the trip takes 4.0/0.80 = 5.0 years. The crew's clocks are present at departure and arrival, so they record the proper time: t₀ = t√(1 − v²/c²) = 5.0 × 0.60 = 3.0 years. The crew are not slower in their own frame; for them the distance is contracted to 2.4 light-years.

questions.stem: A spacecraft is 100 m long when measured at rest. How long does an observer measure it to be as it flies past at 0.60c?
questions.explanation: l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²) = 100 × √(1 − 0.36) = 100 × 0.80 = 80 m. Dividing by 0.80 gives 125 m, which would make a moving object longer. Multiplying by 0.64 forgets the square root.

questions.stem: Length contraction affects an object moving at relativistic speed:
options: only along its direction of motion
only at right angles to its motion
equally in every direction
only if it is accelerating
questions.explanation: A moving object is measured to be shorter only in the direction it moves. Its dimensions perpendicular to the motion are unchanged, which is why the mirror separation in a moving light clock is not contracted.

questions.stem: A spacecraft passes Earth at high speed. Who measures the proper length of the spacecraft?
options: Both of them, because length is the same in all frames
Neither of them, because proper length cannot be measured
An astronaut on board, at rest relative to the spacecraft
An observer on Earth, who sees the spacecraft fly past
questions.explanation: Proper length, l₀, is the length measured in the frame where the object is at rest, so the astronaut measures it. The Earth observer measures a contracted length. Length is not absolute in special relativity.

questions.stem: From the frame of a muon moving at 0.995c (γ ≈ 10), the atmosphere it crosses is 15 km thick in Earth's frame. How thick is it in the muon's frame?
options: About 1.5 km
About 150 km
About 15 km
About 0.15 km
questions.explanation: In the muon's frame the atmosphere is moving, so its thickness is contracted: l = l₀/γ ≈ 15/10 = 1.5 km. The muon can cross this in its short proper lifetime. Earth explains the same result with time dilation, and both views agree on how many muons reach the ground.

questions.stem: A proton (rest mass 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 0.60c. What is its relativistic momentum?
options: 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
6.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: p = m₀v/√(1 − v²/c²) = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ × 1.8 × 10⁸/0.80 ≈ 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹. The classical value m₀v is 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, and multiplying by 0.80 instead of dividing gives 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹.

questions.stem: As a particle's speed approaches c, what happens to its relativistic momentum?
options: It reaches a maximum of m₀c
It falls back towards zero
It stays equal to m₀v
It increases without limit
questions.explanation: p = γm₀v, and γ grows without bound as v approaches c, so the momentum increases without limit. Classically p = m₀v would level off at m₀c, but measurements on fast particles in accelerators agree with the relativistic formula.

questions.stem: Why can't an object with mass be accelerated to the speed of light?
options: Its momentum and energy would become infinite, so infinite work would be needed
Its mass would fall to zero, so a force could no longer act on it
Air resistance always grows faster than any force that could be applied
Its length would grow without limit, so it could not fit in any accelerator
questions.explanation: As v approaches c, γ approaches infinity, so the momentum and the energy needed to reach that speed grow without limit. A finite force acting for a finite time can therefore never get a massive object to c. Particles in accelerators get ever closer to c but never reach it.

questions.stem: An electron is accelerated from 0.90c to 0.99c, and then the same force acts for the same time again. Which statement is correct?
options: Its momentum stops increasing once its speed has reached 0.99c, the limit
Its speed and its momentum both increase by smaller amounts each time
Its momentum rises by the same amount each time, but its speed rises by less and less
Its speed increases by 0.09c each time, so it eventually exceeds the speed of light
questions.explanation: A constant force for a fixed time gives a fixed change in momentum, FΔt = Δp. Near c, γ rises steeply, so each equal increase in momentum gives an ever smaller increase in speed, and v approaches but never reaches c. Momentum has no upper limit.

questions.stem: In 1971, Hafele and Keating flew caesium atomic clocks around the world on commercial airliners and compared them with clocks left on the ground. What did they find?
options: The flown clocks stopped working at high altitude, so no comparison was possible
The flown clocks differed from the ground clocks by amounts agreeing with relativity
The flown clocks kept exactly the same time as the ground clocks, as classical physics predicts
The flown clocks gained hours compared with the ground clocks because of air resistance
questions.explanation: The clocks flown eastward and westward were found to differ from the ground clocks by tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, in agreement with the predictions of relativity (including the effect of gravity on time). The effect is tiny at airliner speeds but measurable with atomic clocks.

questions.stem: Which observation is direct evidence for time dilation?
options: Light from distant stars takes many years to reach observers on Earth
The double-slit pattern shows that light behaves as a wave when it passes through slits
Satellites in higher orbits travel more slowly than satellites in lower orbits
More muons from the upper atmosphere reach the ground than their proper lifetime allows
questions.explanation: Measured muon numbers at mountain and sea level show that fast muons survive far longer in Earth's frame than their proper lifetime of about 2.2 µs, as time dilation predicts. Light travel time and orbital speeds are explained by classical physics.

questions.stem: A particle accelerator stores unstable particles moving at very high speed. Compared with identical particles at rest, the moving particles:
options: decay sooner, because their high speed makes them unstable
decay at exactly the same rate, as measured in the laboratory
never decay at all, because time stops at high speed
survive longer before decaying, as measured in the laboratory
questions.explanation: In the laboratory frame the moving particles' internal clocks run slow by the factor γ, so they live longer on average, as experiments confirm. Time does not stop for any particle with mass, because it cannot reach the speed of light.

questions.stem: Which quantity has the same value for every inertial observer, according to special relativity?
options: The time between two events
The length of a moving rod
The momentum of a moving particle
The speed of light in a vacuum
questions.explanation: The second postulate makes c the same for all inertial observers. Time intervals, lengths and momenta all depend on the observer's frame, which is the basis of time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum.

questions.stem: Observer A is on a spacecraft moving at 0.60c relative to observer B on Earth. Each looks at the other's clock. What does each conclude?
options: Neither sees any difference, because both are in inertial frames
Each measures the other's clock running slow by a factor of 1.25
A measures B's clock running fast, and B measures A's running slow
Both agree that A's clock runs slow and B's clock runs fast
questions.explanation: By the first postulate neither frame is special, so each observer measures the other's moving clock running slow, with γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1.25. This is consistent because the two observers also disagree about simultaneity.

questions.stem: A clock on a fast-moving spacecraft records a proper time of 2.0 hours. The spacecraft moves at 0.60c relative to Earth. How much time passes on Earth?
options: 2.0 hours
2.5 hours
1.6 hours
3.3 hours
questions.explanation: t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²) = 2.0/0.80 = 2.5 hours. Multiplying by 0.80 gives 1.6 hours, which would make the Earth interval shorter than the proper time, and dividing by 0.60 gives 3.3 hours.

questions.stem: Which statement about relativistic effects is correct when they are viewed from an external frame?
options: A moving clock runs slow, a moving rod is unchanged, and momentum equals exactly m₀v
A moving clock runs slow, a moving rod is shorter along its motion, and momentum exceeds m₀v
A moving clock runs fast, a moving rod is longer along its motion, and momentum exceeds m₀v
A moving clock runs slow, a moving rod is shorter across its motion, and momentum is below m₀v
questions.explanation: Seen from outside, time dilation makes moving clocks run slow, length contraction shortens objects only along their motion, and relativistic momentum γm₀v is greater than the classical m₀v. All three effects depend on the same factor, γ.

questions.stem: Which observer measures the proper time between a muon's creation and its decay?
options: Any observer, because all measure the same
An observer moving along with the muon
An observer standing on the ground
An observer moving at the speed of light
questions.explanation: Proper time is measured by a clock present at both events. The muon is created and decays at the same place in its own frame, so a clock moving with it records the proper time. A ground observer measures a longer, dilated time.

questions.stem: A rod moving at 0.80c along its length is measured by an observer to be 3.0 m long. What is its proper length?
questions.explanation: The measured length is contracted: l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²), so l₀ = 3.0/0.60 = 5.0 m. Multiplying by 0.60 gives 1.8 m, which treats 3.0 m as the proper length, and dividing by 0.64 forgets the square root.

questions.stem: A crew's clocks record a trip of 2.0 hours while clocks on Earth record 2.5 hours for the same trip. How fast is the spacecraft moving relative to Earth?
questions.explanation: The Lorentz factor is 2.5/2.0 = 1.25, so √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.80 and v²/c² = 0.36, giving v = 0.60c. Stopping at v²/c² gives 0.36c, and 0.80c confuses √(1 − v²/c²) with v/c.

questions.stem: Two space stations are 2.4 × 10¹¹ m apart in their own rest frame. A spacecraft travels from one to the other at 0.80c. What distance between the stations does the crew measure?
questions.explanation: In the crew's frame the stations are moving, so the distance between them is contracted: 2.4 × 10¹¹ × √(1 − 0.64) = 2.4 × 10¹¹ × 0.60 ≈ 1.4 × 10¹¹ m. Multiplying by 0.80 gives 1.9 × 10¹¹ m, which confuses v/c with the contraction factor.
